back: A dimension along which an object, individual or group may be categorized (e.g. income, height, weight) — a characteristic that can be measured and may vary along a continuum.
The causal factor in a cause-and-effect relationship. Sometimes treated as the constant for the problem at hand.
The effect in a cause-and-effect relationship; determined by other variables. In sociology, usually a form of human action (attitude or behaviour).
A test factor introduced to determine whether it produces the dependent variable through its interaction with the independent factor. Not directly seen or controlled.

The study of a single instance of a phenomenon, either for its own sake (e.g. a particular person or strike) or as a research design that takes a single case and uses a variety of methods to study it.
A research subject — the person from whom the researcher wants to elicit information. A respondent answers a questionnaire or a request for information.

A form containing questions administered to a number of people mainly to obtain information and record opinions. Used to examine population characteristics, attitudes, relationships between variables, and to test theories.
A face-to-face method of collecting social data at the individual level. Higher response rate than postal questionnaires but can introduce interviewer bias.
A method of sociological research involving the administration of questionnaires to a population being studied.
Taking a proportion of individuals or cases from a larger population, studied as representative of the population as a whole.
The dependability of data collected, or of the test or measurement used to collect it. A reliable measure gives the same results if the same individuals are measured more than once.
The extent to which a measure, indicator or method of data collection possesses the quality of being sound or true as far as can be judged.
An idea, or a guess, about a given state of affairs, put forward as a basis of empirical testing.
The use of multiple research methods as a way of producing more reliable empirical data than is available from any single method used in isolation.

The explicit procedures used in collecting empirical data — a strategic plan setting out the broad outline, methods of data collection and analysis, and how the strategy addresses the aims of the study.

Accounts of the external world held to represent the world as it exists independently of our conceptions. Knowledge claimed to meet criteria of validity and reliability, and held to be free from bias.
The perspective of the person (subject); lack of objectivity. Often used pejoratively within positivist sociology to derogate biased observation or methodology.
Data that are not in numerical form — descriptive accounts of observations, interviews or written material.
Data in numerical form, obtained through enumeration and measurement.
A research procedure in which the data collected are prepared for counting and tabulation by classification and codification.
A research technique used to describe and analyze objectively, systematically and quantitatively the content of written, spoken or pictorial communications.
The percentage of an eligible random sample that agrees to participate in an interview survey.
Repetition of the same basic study or experiment to check its accuracy or to estimate the experimental error.

The scientific method (associated with Auguste Comte). Treats social phenomena as a reality existing independently of the observer and uses procedures of the natural sciences to collect and analyze data, phrased in terms of variables and statistics.
Max Weber's method of 'interpretative understanding' for studying human behaviour. The humanistic orientation chiefly describes, usually in highly subjective terms, behavioural phenomena.

A systematic collection of facts about people living in a specific geographic, cultural, or administrative area. Generalizations are drawn from a sample of social particulars about the entire universe.
A type of observation in which the observer plays an active role in the behaviour being studied; expected to give greater depth from personal experience in the natural setting.
A type of observation in which the observer takes a totally passive and non-involved part in the behaviour being observed.
A casual and informal type of observation that involves no standardization of observational techniques and no control over pertinent variables.
A formal and precise type of observation that places controls on both the observer and the observed phenomenon, usually involving instruments and refined procedures.
Experimentation conducted in the true context of the behaviour under study.
Observation and/or experimentation conducted in the somewhat artificial confines of a laboratory.
A research method in which selected groups participate in focused discussion on a research issue.
Research carried out in the field rather than the laboratory or library — investigation of real-life situations through observation and informal or unstructured interviewing.
A type of research design in which information about the past is gathered systematically.

A method that takes theories from existing perspectives (Marxism, functionalism, conflict, consensus) and derives hypotheses that are tested against evidence collected in the field or from the library.

A descriptive method involving observation and recording of history, geography, social organization, economy, political system, culture and religion of the people under study. Simple but can lead to ethnocentrism.
First-hand information collected by an investigator directly from fieldwork, survey research, observation or opinion polling.
Information gathered from secondary sources such as statistical records, documents or 'existing material'.

Seeks the facts or causes of social phenomena with little regard for the subjective states of individuals. According to Durkheim, the sociologist should consider 'social facts' as 'things' that exercise external coercive influence on human behaviour.

Concerned with understanding human behaviour from the actor's own frame of reference. Important reality is what people claim it to be. Methods: participant observation, open-ended interviewing, personal documents.

Concerned with elementary forms and processes of social behaviour — informal interpersonal behaviour in face-to-face contexts and small groups. Methods most applied: the experiment and participant observation.

Also called systematic sociology. Studies society as a whole, concerned with broad-scale analysis of formal, structured processes typical of complex organizations. Methods: historical-comparative method, interview and questionnaire.

The dominant theoretical orientation in sociology. Society is conceived as a system of inter-related parts working interdependently; stability, equilibrium and harmonious function are maintained by shared values and beliefs (consensus).

Antithetical to functionalism. Focuses on change and revolution. Assumes the fundamental dynamics of human life are dissensus and competition. Continuous inevitable competition for scarce resources — power, wealth, prestige.
A form of conflict theory closely based on Marx's critique of the capitalist system and on his premise of class conflict.

A theory of human action and interaction that emphasizes the use of symbols and language. Focuses on individuals as social actors rather than the system. W.I. Thomas: 'If men define situations as real, they are real in their consequences.'
The study of the methods people in society use to make sense of what is going on around them. A variety of symbolic interaction.

Focuses on elementary forms of social behaviour — the goals and motives of participants in social interaction. People are depicted as rational creatures in a give-and-take process of rewards and costs.
The 'give-and-take' phenomenon alleged to be the basic dimension of social behaviour. A key concept of Social Exchange Theory (Lévi-Strauss, George Homans).
Oriented to the study of morally complex forms of social interaction. Uses Verstehen to uncover the 'meaning context' in which people and their actions exist (Weber).
An evolutionary view that traditional societies change their basic structure through economic development and industrialization in order to survive. Change occurs through structural differentiation.

Some piece of social behaviour that causes public friction and/or private misery and calls for collective action to solve it — a set of conditions that the majority or a substantial minority disapprove as morally wrong.
An issue concerned with the explanation of the nature and dynamics of social behaviour — not with the development of strategy and techniques for the control or change of social phenomena.
The state of happiness, comfort, and freedom from want. In a pure sociological sense, welfare is a 'community-action' approach to solving social problems.

The ability to appreciate that the 'troubles' that affect the individual are the outcome of much wider arrangements within which their life is lived out — personal troubles are connected with public issues of social structure.
Discrimination or prejudice based on a person's age, especially against older adults.
A pre-judgment or unsupported opinion usually involving negative stereotypes about a group.
Unjust or prejudicial treatment of people on the grounds of group membership.

A group of people who, because of their physical or cultural characteristics, are singled out from the others in the society in which they live for differential and unequal treatment, and who therefore regard themselves as objects of collective discrimination.
Prejudice, discrimination or antagonism directed against a person or people on the basis of their membership in a particular racial or ethnic group, typically one that is a minority or marginalized.
The state of not having enough material possessions or income for a person's basic needs.
Replaces ethnocentrism with cultural relativism — the realization that customs, traditions, religions and cultures of others are not bad simply because they are different.
An educative discipline that satisfies the yearnings of curious people. Educates people about the societies they live in, beyond common sensual knowledge and speculation.
The everyday involvement of sociologists in the affairs and activities of organizations, businesses and governments — specifying implications and consequences of alternative types of social policy.

Young graduates in the discipline are particularly attracted to this field of youth probation, using sociological understanding and personal guidance to steer young offenders towards productive adulthood.
Activities that involve screening of applicants for jobs in industry, helping prepare job descriptions, and coordinating or mediating inter-departmental matters.
